\section[passus, passūs]{passus, passūs — a pace}

\label{lesson:LA-C218-passus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a vehicle, then the Latin for a chariot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: passus, passūs}
\textbf{passus, passūs} — \textquotedblleft{}a pace\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{passus} is built on \emph{pandō}, \textquotedblleft{}to spread out, to stretch\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1): a pace as the stretch of the legs. A Roman mile was \emph{mīlle passūs}, \textquotedblleft{}a thousand paces\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{passus, passūs}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{passus, passūs}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{passus, passūs}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a vehicle, then the Latin for a chariot, then say \emph{passus, passūs} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does passus, passūs mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A pace\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[testis, testis]{testis, testis — a witness}

\label{lesson:LA-C218-testis}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a chariot, then the Latin for a pace.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: testis, testis}
\textbf{testis, testis} — \textquotedblleft{}a witness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{testis} is usually explained as an old compound, \emph{*tri-stis}, \textquotedblleft{}the third who stands by\textquotedblright{}, from the root of \emph{trēs}, \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{stō}, \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{}: a witness as the third party.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[poena, poenae]{poena, poenae — a punishment}

\label{lesson:LA-C218-poena}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a witness, then the Latin for a defendant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: poena, poenae}
\textbf{poena, poenae} — \textquotedblleft{}a punishment\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{poena} was borrowed from Greek \emph{poinē}, \textquotedblleft{}a fine, blood-money\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), which is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*kwoyneh2}, \textquotedblleft{}penalty\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1). English \emph{pain} comes from it through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[crīmen, crīminis]{crīmen, crīminis — a charge, a crime}

\label{lesson:LA-C218-crimen}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a defendant, then the Latin for a punishment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: crīmen, crīminis}
\textbf{crīmen, crīminis} — \textquotedblleft{}a charge, a crime\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{crīmen} belongs with \emph{cernō}, \textquotedblleft{}to sift, to decide\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), and is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*kreymn}, \textquotedblleft{}a verdict, a sifting\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1): first a judgement, then a charge.
\end{cousinweb}
